lead: Three days before Pentecost both readings speak of what God has promised and how surely he keeps it. Hebrews calls our hope “a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul”, fixed where Jesus has gone before us. In John, Jesus stands up at the feast of Booths and promises rivers of living water, and the evangelist explains: “he said this about the Spirit.” Today the Church also remembers Mar Ishaq of Antioch, a teacher and poet of the Syriac Church. The key words are anchor and living water.

r.h: Hope, a sure and steadfast anchor
set: Hebrews is a sermon in written form for Christians who were growing weary. Just before this passage the author warns against falling away and then encourages his readers: God is not unjust, he will not forget your love (6:10). To show that the promise is certain he goes back to Abraham, to whom God swore an oath after the near sacrifice of Isaac (Genesis 22:16–17).
str: vv. 13–15: God's oath to Abraham, and Abraham's patience.
vv. 16–18: why an oath: two unchangeable things, the promise and the oath.
vv. 19–20: hope as an anchor, reaching behind the curtain, where Jesus has entered.
kw: In the ancient world the anchor was a picture of steadiness and hope. Early Christians carved it on tombs in the Roman catacombs, sometimes shaped like a cross. Here the anchor is not dropped into the sea below but cast upward, into heaven.

A runner sent ahead, or a scout who goes first so that others can follow. Jesus has not entered heaven only for himself. He has gone ahead “on our behalf”, and where he is, his people are meant to come.
vv: When God made a promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself,
The words of Genesis 22:16 are “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord.” God binds himself with his own name.
We have this hope, a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters the inner shrine behind the curtain,
The curtain is the veil before the Holy of Holies in the tabernacle, where the high priest entered only once a year (Leviticus 16). Our hope reaches into the very presence of God.
where Jesus, a forerunner on our behalf, has entered, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.
This verse leads into chapter 7, where Melchizedek, the priest-king who brought out bread and wine (Genesis 14:18), becomes a figure of the eternal priesthood of Christ.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a lesson in Christian hope. The Catechism calls hope the virtue by which we desire the Kingdom of heaven and eternal life, placing our trust in Christ's promises and relying on the grace of the Holy Spirit, and it quotes this very verse about the anchor (CCC 1817, 1820). Hope is not a guess about the future. It rests on God's word, and God does not go back on his word.

r.h: Let anyone who is thirsty come to me
set: The scene is the feast of Booths (Tabernacles), the autumn harvest feast in Jerusalem (John 7:2). Later Jewish sources (the Mishnah, tractate Sukkah) describe how on each day of the feast water was drawn from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar, with prayer for the rains. Many scholars think this rite stands behind Jesus' cry on “the great day”. The feast also recalled the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17; Numbers 20).
str: vv. 37–38: Jesus' cry: come, drink; rivers of living water.
v. 39: the evangelist's comment: this is the Spirit, not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified.
kw: In everyday Greek and Hebrew, “living water” is fresh running water from a spring, not water kept in a cistern. Jesus used the same words to the Samaritan woman (4:10). Here John says plainly what it means: the Holy Spirit.

In John, Jesus is “glorified” in his hour: his Cross, Resurrection and return to the Father (12:23; 17:1). The Spirit is given from the glorified Christ. On the Cross water flows from his side (19:34); on Easter evening he breathes the Spirit on the disciples (20:22).
vv: Let anyone who is thirsty come to me,
Jesus stands and cries out, as a teacher who wants everyone to hear. The invitation echoes Isaiah 55:1: “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters.”
Out of the believer’s heart shall flow rivers of living water.

The Greek is literally “out of his belly”. Ancient punctuation can be read two ways: the rivers flow from the believer, or from Christ, if we read “let the one who believes in me drink” together with v. 37. Many Fathers took it of Christ, the rock from whom the water flows; both readings are found, and both are true in their own way. No single verse of the Old Testament says these exact words; John seems to gather passages such as Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Zechariah 14:8.
for as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
This does not mean the Spirit did not exist. Some manuscripts add “given”, and that is the sense: the Spirit had not yet been poured out as the gift of the risen Lord.
ch: The Church hears in this Gospel the promise of Pentecost and of Baptism. The Catechism names water among the symbols of the Holy Spirit and links it to the water from Christ's pierced side (CCC 694). Every baptized Christian has drunk of this water. The same Spirit wants to flow out through us to others, so that our homes and parishes become springs and not stagnant pools.

qa: Who was Mar Ishaq of Antioch?

He was a Syriac teacher and poet, usually placed in the fifth century, and many metrical homilies (memre) have come down under his name. Scholars think that the writings under the name Isaac may come from more than one author of that time. Our Church honours him as a Malpan, a teacher of the faith in song.
study: What anchors my soul when life is stormy: God's promise, or something smaller?
Where do I feel thirsty in my spiritual life, and how can I come to Jesus to drink before Pentecost?
